source: Lakatos (1963) Proofs and Refutations (I), Brit. J. Phil. Sci. 14(53)
finding: Lakatos names the moves of refutation-driven conjecture revision: surrender, monster-barring, exception-barring, monster-adjusting, lemma-incorporation, and proofs and refutations. Counterexamples drive change in concepts, conjectures and proofs.
numbers: Section list read: criticism of the conjecture by global counterexamples, criticism of the proof by local counterexamples; Euler V-E+F=2 case.
limits: Part I only. A rational reconstruction of history, not an empirical study.
agent_relevance: Vocabulary for a counterexample-handling operator. Also flags monster-barring (redefining terms to save a claim) as a failure the agent must detect.

source: Martin and Pease (2013) Mathematical practice, crowdsourcing, and social machines
finding: Computational reading of Polya and Lakatos: counterexamples trigger six revision methods. Monster-barring and monster-adjusting exploit vague concept definitions. Links to Colton's HR theory-formation system and Pease's computational model of Lakatos-style reasoning.
numbers: Picture-frame polyhedron V-E+F = 16-32+16 = 0; Kepler star polyhedron 12-30+12 = -6 or 32-90+60 = 2 depending on how faces are counted.
limits: Secondary source; no LLM data. Pease thesis (2009) is cited but was not opened.
agent_relevance: Older AI lineage (HR, Lakatos-style rule systems) ran conjecture-refute loops in code. A precedent for a program-controlled refutation loop.

source: Chuharski et al. (2024) Mining Math Conjectures from LLMs: A Pruning Approach
finding: GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 Flash proposed group-theory (solubilizer) conjectures and wrote GAP code to test them. Refuted conjectures were fed back as known-false, a Lakatos-style loop.
numbers: 757 outputs, 420 unique (55.48%). 109 (25.95%) refuted by a counterexample; 40 (9.52%) had no counterexample found; 271 (64.52%) had code that would not run. Surviving share: ChatGPT 26.60%, Gemini 4.64%, Claude 4.49%.
limits: One narrow domain. One author judged novelty. Survivors may be those easy to code, not good ones. Two code repairs allowed.
agent_relevance: A running refuter prunes most model conjectures (G2, G3). About half the model output was duplicate.

source: Chuharski et al. (2024) Mining Math Conjectures from LLMs: A Pruning Approach
finding: Conjecture diversity stayed low. More trials and more prompt variants did not raise it.
numbers: Mean cosine self-similarity: ChatGPT 0.2911, Claude 0.4238, Gemini 0.2451. Similarity to the source literature: 0.13 to 0.21 (means by model).
limits: Embedding similarity is a crude diversity proxy.
agent_relevance: Resampling one model gives repeats (G4). Diversity must come from structured operators, such as what-if-not changes to givens.

source: Chuharski et al. (2024) Mining Math Conjectures from LLMs: A Pruning Approach
finding: Models differed in how testable their conjectures were. ChatGPT often restricted the groups it considered and conjectured about solubilizer size only.
numbers: Non-executable code: Gemini 81.86%, Claude 49.44%, ChatGPT 37.76%.
limits: About 250 outputs per model.
agent_relevance: Survivor bias: tested conjectures are the easy-to-test ones. The agent should log untestable conjectures instead of dropping them.

source: Sivakumar et al. (2025) Conjecturing: An Overlooked Step in Formal Mathematical Reasoning
finding: ConjectureBench separates conjecturing (state the answer or bound) from autoformalisation. Standalone conjecturing is very weak.
numbers: 457 problems. Standalone equiv-rfl pass@1: GPT-4.1 3.28% (15/457), DeepSeek-V3.1 3.72% (17/457). pass@10: 5.04% and 5.70%. Proof-type answers: 0/114 at pass@1 for both.
limits: Strict equivalence metric. Authors saw signs of data contamination (helper names such as IsMagicSquare that exist only in the gold formalisation).
agent_relevance: Stating the claim is a separate weak skill. Do not let a prover step quietly stand in for it.

source: Sivakumar et al. (2025) Conjecturing: An Overlooked Step in Formal Mathematical Reasoning
finding: Withholding the conjecture ('unseen') lowers end-to-end autoformalisation, so earlier scores were overestimated.
numbers: Average 23.7% drop from seen to unseen. GPT-4.1 baseline LLM-Grader@10: 36.32 (seen) to 20.35 (unseen).
limits: The grader is an LLM judge (Qwen3-14B calibrated to human annotators).
agent_relevance: Gives a measured size for the effect of leaking the answer. Check whether benchmarks hand over the claim.

source: Sivakumar et al. (2025) Conjecturing: An Overlooked Step in Formal Mathematical Reasoning
finding: LEAN-FIRE (informal chain of thought plus Lean-of-thought) helped conjecturing only with few-shot examples. Removing them removed most of the gain.
numbers: Authors report GPT-4.1 pass@10 up to +28% in the unseen setting. 13 PutnamBench no-answer problems autoformalised by GPT-4.1 and 7 by DeepSeek-V3.1 (BEq+). Net mean gain +3.01% at pass@1, slight decline at pass@10.
limits: Few-shot examples can push template errors in the unseen setting. Gains small on the strict metric.
agent_relevance: Scaffold structure alone did little; worked examples did the work. Favours example libraries over extra reasoning rules.

source: Onda et al. (2025) LeanConjecturer: Automatic Generation of Mathematical Conjectures for Theorem Proving
finding: LeanConjecturer: rule-based context extraction plus LLM statement writing, iterated, with Lean parsing, a Mathlib novelty check and an aesop triviality filter.
numbers: 40 Mathlib seed files: 12,289 conjectures; 10,950 valid; 4,130 novel; 3,776 non-trivial; 103.25 novel per seed on average; 25 of 40 files hit the 15-iteration cap.
limits: 'Non-trivial' only means aesop fails; false statements are included. No human interest rating.
agent_relevance: Cheap code filters (parse, novelty, triviality) turn raw model posing into a usable pool. Fits G5: code selects.

source: Onda et al. (2025) LeanConjecturer: Automatic Generation of Mathematical Conjectures for Theorem Proving
finding: One instruction in the prompt changed output volume sharply.
numbers: Seed Mathlib.Algebra.Group.Commutator: without 'as many as possible' 1 total, 0 valid; with it 412 total, 392 valid, 108 non-trivial.
limits: One seed file.
agent_relevance: Posing output is sensitive to small wording. Test the prompt per seed.

source: Onda et al. (2025) LeanConjecturer: Automatic Generation of Mathematical Conjectures for Theorem Proving
finding: Training on self-posed conjectures with GRPO gave modest local gains that did not transfer.
numbers: 192 topology conjectures, 128 samples each. DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B proof rate 2285/24576 to 3657/24576 after 10 epochs; problems solved 47/192 to 49/192, 50/192 after 34 epochs. Alpha-open test set: 9/14 to 8/14 at 10 epochs, 9/14 at 34.
limits: Training set not filtered (true and false mixed). Transfer test only 14 problems.
agent_relevance: Posing helps the poser's own distribution. Little sign of transfer. Not directly usable for a no-training scaffold.

source: Onda et al. (2025) LeanConjecturer: Automatic Generation of Mathematical Conjectures for Theorem Proving
finding: The context shown to the conjecturer changes diversity: only proven theorems gave similar patterns; all conjectured statements gave more varied ones.
numbers: Qualitative; no counts given.
limits: Author observation, not tested.
agent_relevance: What is shown as context shapes proposal diversity. A design lever for the agent.

source: Kasaura et al. (2025/2026) Discovering New Theorems via LLMs with In-Context Proof Learning in Lean (CPL)
finding: Conjecturing-Proving Loop (CPL): generate conjectures, try to prove in Lean 4, feed verified results back as context. Compared with single-pass statement-plus-proof generation (SL). Both used o3.
numbers: 20 runs each, 14M-token budget. CPL averaged 106 theorems and found the target theorem (intersection of two alpha-open sets is alpha-open) in 5/20 runs. SL averaged 328 theorems and found it 0/20. Fisher exact p = 0.024.
limits: One target theorem, chosen by the authors. Notions anonymised to block memory.
agent_relevance: Separating posing from proving and keeping verified results in context found a hard result that volume generation missed. Quality beats count.

source: Kasaura et al. (2025/2026) Discovering New Theorems via LLMs with In-Context Proof Learning in Lean (CPL)
finding: Verified self-generated context raises later proof success.
numbers: Re-proving 2,123 CPL theorems: 99% (2106/2123) with earlier library as context vs 91% (1935/2123) with definitions only. Without in-context learning, CPL made 309 theorems and SL 941; neither found the target.
limits: The same model proves its own statements, which is easier than outside problems.
agent_relevance: Supports a persistent store of verified lemmas inside the agent loop.

source: Kasaura et al. (2025/2026) Discovering New Theorems via LLMs with In-Context Proof Learning in Lean (CPL)
finding: Natural-language check on the true target theorem: models wrongly called it false.
numbers: GPT-4o said false 10 times and gave wrong proofs 6 times. o3 never gave a wrong proof but always judged it false.
limits: Small number of trials.
agent_relevance: Models also wrongly refute true claims. A refuter needs a witness that code checks (G3), not an opinion.

source: Dong and Ma (2025) STP: Self-play LLM Theorem Provers with Iterative Conjecturing and Proving
finding: Self-play conjecturer and prover. The conjecturer is rewarded for statements barely provable by the current prover.
numbers: 51.3B tokens in Lean; 3.6M generated conjectures. 28.5% of LeanWorkbook proved vs 13.2% prior best (expert iteration). miniF2F-test 65.0% (pass@3200), ProofNet-test 23.9%, PutnamBench 8/644. At 11.4% pass rate, expert iteration got 131 correct of 2.5M proofs; at least 47% of STP conjectures were proved.
limits: A training method, not a prompt scaffold.
agent_relevance: Value of posing at the edge of ability. An agent could pose sub-lemmas that are neither trivial nor hopeless.

source: Poesia et al. (2024) Learning Formal Mathematics From Intrinsic Motivation (Minimo)
finding: Minimo poses its own conjectures (type-directed constrained decoding makes them well-formed by construction) and proves them, starting from axioms only.
numbers: 3 domains: propositional logic, arithmetic, group theory. Only about 10 to 20% of initial conjectures were proven. Without hindsight relabeling the conjecturer drifted to easy statements and could not leave that regime.
limits: Small models trained from scratch in axiom domains.
agent_relevance: Failure to guard: self-posed problems drift easy. Well-formedness by construction removes ill-posed output.

source: Xu et al. (2026) MathDuels: a self-play benchmark that grows
finding: Models author problems and solve others' problems. Author quality comes from how hard their problems are (Rasch model). Authoring and solving are only partly the same skill.
numbers: 19 frontier models, 570 problems; 11 excluded as ill-posed, 559 valid; 10,062 solve observations. The best solver was not the best overall model. 27.6% of 275 problems from the two newest models beat at least one prior top-3 solver vs 8.0% for the other 17 authors.
limits: Difficulty is measured by other models. An LLM verifier decides well-posedness.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a good solver is a good poser. Newer models pose harder problems.

source: Xu et al. (2026) MathDuels: a self-play benchmark that grows
finding: Posing recipe: meta-prompting, problem generation, difficulty amplification, then an independent verifier removes ill-posed items.
numbers: 11 of 570 problems (1.9%) removed by the verifier. Verifier backbone agreement checked on 414 problems.
limits: Verifier is a model.
agent_relevance: A concrete posing pipeline. The validity gate is the part to copy.

source: Petrov, Dekoninck, Vechev (2025) BrokenMath: a benchmark for sycophancy in theorem proving with LLMs
finding: Refutation side: models often write proofs of false statements (sycophancy). 2025 competition problems were perturbed into false versions and expert-reviewed.
numbers: Best model, GPT-5, sycophantic in 29.0% of cases. Self-sycophancy (flawed problems the model itself posed) up to 15.6 points worse. Best-of-n cut sycophancy by 5.4 points (Qwen3-4B) and 8.6 (Qwen3-235B).
limits: LLM judge (GPT-5-mini with 3-vote majority, 95% accurate). False statements produced by an LLM edit.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that models do not test claims by default. Needs a forced validity check.

source: Petrov, Dekoninck, Vechev (2025) BrokenMath: a benchmark for sycophancy in theorem proving with LLMs
finding: Mitigations reduced but did not remove sycophancy.
numbers: Asking the model to check the problem first lowered rates but not to zero. Confidence heuristics: only Low@16 on Qwen3-235B gave a 6.4 point drop; others negligible or negative.
limits: Open models only for mitigation tests.
agent_relevance: A 'check the claim first' instruction is a cheap partial fix. A code-run counterexample search is stronger.

source: Adamczewski (2026) OEIS Open: how many conjectures can language models turn into theorems?
finding: Language models with Lean checking and minimal tools resolve many open conjectures.
numbers: 492 OEIS conjectures: Claude Opus 4.8 30% (147 at $50 per attempt), GPT-5.5 26%, Gemini 3.5 Flash 22%. Lite set of 100: best 44% at $200. Cost per resolved conjecture $6 to $10 average, $47 max. 476,000 arXiv papers as a tool gave no gain; neither did more elaborate agent loops.
limits: Conjectures are of uncertain significance and mostly little studied. Misformalisation and training-data leak risks.
agent_relevance: Literature access and fancy loops gave nothing; a verifier plus budget did. Fits 'code checks, model fills a slot'.

source: Tsoukalas et al. (2026) Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search
finding: Large-scale Lean agent on open problems. A basic agent alternating generation and Lean verification replicated the Erdos successes but cost more on the hardest.
numbers: 9 of 353 open Erdos problems resolved; 44 of 492 OEIS conjectures proved.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read closely.
agent_relevance: Verification-grounded loops produce real new results. The loop matters more than the prompt.

source: Xie, Ye, Zhang (2026) ALPS: Measuring Valid Creativity in LLMs with Mathematical Construction
finding: ALPS measures valid creativity (original and provably correct) with equational laws that need a construction or a no-model proof, checked automatically.
numbers: Eight prover configurations solve 2.2% of 4,141 laws; 20x budget adds 0.6%. Best reasoning model succeeds on 14% of the proof side and none on the construction side. 97.2% of the pool unresolved.
limits: Narrow domain; model-version specific.
agent_relevance: Models fail when a tailored construction is needed. Building the counterexample is the hard half of refutation.

source: Li et al. (2026) RIDE: Difficulty Evolving Perturbation with Item Response Theory for Mathematical Reasoning
finding: Rewriting problems into harder variants (changing the givens, close to what-if-not on conditions) lowers accuracy.
numbers: Average 21.73% drop across 26 LLMs on competition-level benchmarks.
limits: Variants are tuned with item response theory to be harder but answerable; not a human-style what-if-not list.
agent_relevance: Changing a problem's conditions exposes fragile reasoning. Usable as a robustness probe and a posing operator.
